sources.title: Interpretations of Probability
sources.publisher: Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
sources.version: First published 21 October 2002; substantive revision 16 November 2023
sources.locator: Kolmogorov's axiomatisation, covering non-negativity, normalisation, and finite additivity over disjoint events; the ratio definition of conditional probability for a conditioning event of positive probability; the finite and hypothetical frequency interpretations and their stated problems, including the reference-class and single-case objections
sources.license: Copyright 2023 Alan Hájek; freely readable under the encyclopedia's stated terms, with no open-content reuse licence displayed

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only to verify the standard probability axioms, the ratio definition of conditional probability, the long-run relative-frequency reading of probability, and the recorded limits of that reading. No wording, example, table, figure, or organisation from the entry is reused; every worked case in the lesson is original and invented.

sources.title: Evaluation of measurement data — Guide to the expression of uncertainty in measurement (JCGM 100:2008), Annex C: Basic statistical terms and concepts
creators: Joint Committee for Guides in Metrology, Working Group 1
sources.publisher: Bureau International des Poids et Mesures
sources.version: JCGM 100:2008, first edition September 2008; GUM 1995 with minor corrections
sources.locator: Annex C, clause C.2.1 defining probability as a real number in the scale 0 to 1 attached to a random event with a note relating it to a long-run relative frequency of occurrence; clause C.2.3 with its note that the probability over the whole set of values equals 1; clause C.3.7 defining statistical independence as a joint distribution equal to the product of the individual distributions
sources.license: Copyright JCGM 2008, all rights reserved as displayed on the document; no open-content licence is relied on here

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only to verify that a probability is a number between 0 and 1 attached to a random event and relatable to a long-run relative frequency, that probability over the whole outcome set is 1, and that independence is characterised by a product. No clause wording, example, note, table, or figure is reproduced, adapted, or redistributed.

sources.version: Encyclopedia of Mathematics wiki article, adapted from an original article in the Encyclopaedia of Mathematics, ISBN 1402006098
sources.locator: Definition of the conditional probability of an event relative to a conditioning event of positive probability as the ratio of the probability of their intersection to the probability of the conditioning event

sources.version: Encyclopedia of Mathematics wiki article, adapted from an original article in the Encyclopaedia of Mathematics, ISBN 1402006098

sources.title: Sensitivity, Specificity, and Predictive Values: Foundations, Pliabilities, and Pitfalls in Research and Practice
sources.locator: Abstract; the introduction's definitions of predictive values as probabilities attached to a test result; the passage separating the test-focused question from the person-focused question; the passage naming confusion of the inverse; the statement that cell entries depend on test stringency and on the prevalence of the target condition in the sample; conclusion

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only to verify that detection measures condition on a person's true state while predictive values condition on the test result, that predictive values depend on how common the condition is in the tested group, that performance estimates can vary with threshold and tested-sample composition, and that reversing the two is the error known as confusion of the inverse. No wording, analogy, example, table, or figure from the review is reused; the two invented clinics and all counts are original.

sources.title: Statistical tests, P values, confidence intervals, and power: a guide to misinterpretations
sources.locator: Introduction, defining the P value as a probability computed under the assumption that every model assumption including the test hypothesis is correct; the listed misinterpretation that the P value is the probability that the test hypothesis is true, and its correction

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only to verify the direction of the conditional in a P value: that it assumes the tested hypothesis and the surrounding model rather than reporting the probability of that hypothesis given the data. No wording, numbered item, example, or organisation is reused, and this lesson does not teach hypothesis testing.

sources.title: Assessment of cognitive biases and biostatistics knowledge of medical residents: a multicenter, cross-sectional questionnaire study
sources.locator: Abstract, reporting 153 respondents at a 76.5 per cent response rate and 54.2 per cent correct on the gambler's-fallacy vignette; introduction description of the gambler's fallacy as expecting a long-run deviation to be corrected in the short term; results reporting the odds ratio relating biostatistics score to correct performance; discussion and conclusion

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only to verify that expecting short-run correction after a run of like outcomes is a documented reasoning error among medical residents, and to record the survey's sample size, response rate, and the reported percentage answering its vignette correctly. The study's clinical vignette is not reproduced, adapted, or paraphrased; every scenario in this lesson is original.
